name: Emergency Messages
title: Emergency Messages
answer: Emergency messages are pre-written templates for situations such as a lockdown, a weather closure or a bus delay, drafted and translated with AI help and reviewed by people before anything happens. When a crisis arrives, staff fill in the details instead of writing from scratch. The aim is to get accurate information to every family at the same time, in a language they read, without losing minutes.

sections.body: Schools face a recurring problem: emergencies demand fast and accurate messages, and writing one from nothing under pressure invites errors. The idea is to prepare templates in advance for the situations a school is most likely to face, such as a lockdown, a weather closure or a bus delay. AI can draft those templates and produce translations ahead of time, with people reviewing the results. When the emergency actually happens, staff only need to fill in the specific details. This turns a rushed writing task into a short, checked editing task.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not divide this practice by grade band, so the same routine applies across a school. Before any emergency, staff build a set of templates for the common situations the school expects, using AI to draft the wording and to translate it. Fluent speakers review each translated template in advance, so reviewed versions exist in every major home language the school serves. Every message must then be approved by an administrator before it goes out, and that approval step is assigned clearly and kept quick so it does not become a bottleneck. During the emergency itself, staff fill in the details rather than composing from scratch.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book offers no study, figure or evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. The case made in the text is practical: reviewed templates in each major home language mean every family receives accurate information at the same time, and the text calls this one of the most valuable uses of preparation. The reasoning about risk is also stated rather than measured, namely that a wrong message during an emergency can cause panic or put people in danger. Readers should treat the approach as sound operational judgement rather than a tested finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Every emergency message must be approved by an administrator before it is sent, because speed matters but accuracy matters more. That approval must be quick and clearly assigned, or the safeguard itself becomes a bottleneck. Translations carry their own risk: fluent speakers must review translated templates before any emergency occurs, since there will be no time to check a translation during a crisis. The decisions about what a message says, who approves it and whether a translation is good enough stay with people, not with the AI that drafted them.
